problems.title: Same Tree
problems.description:
Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, return `true` if they have exactly the same shape and every pair of corresponding nodes holds the same value, otherwise `false`.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Same values, but the single child is on different sides.

constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each tree <= 10^4
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space where h is the tree height
hints: Two trees are equal only if their roots match and their subtrees match.
Compare the roots, then recurse on left with left and right with right. Two empty trees are equal; one empty and one non-empty are not.
isSame(a, b): if both null return true; if exactly one is null or values differ return false; otherwise isSame(a.left, b.left) and isSame(a.right, b.right).

problems.title: Symmetric Tree
problems.description:
Return `true` if a binary tree is a mirror image of itself around its center: the left subtree must be the mirror of the right subtree, both in shape and in values.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: The `3` nodes sit on the same side in both subtrees, so they are not mirrored.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Think of comparing two trees at once rather than one tree against itself.
Two nodes mirror each other if their values match, the left child of one mirrors the right child of the other, and vice versa.
Start with the pair (root.left, root.right). Check null/value conditions, then push (a.left, b.right) and (a.right, b.left).

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.description:
The diameter of a binary tree is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root. Return the diameter of the given tree.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: The path 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 has 3 edges.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: The best path has a highest node; consider each node as that highest point.
Through a node, the longest path equals height(left) + height(right), where height counts nodes below it.
Compute heights bottom-up in one pass, updating a global best with leftHeight + rightHeight at every node. Use an explicit stack to avoid deep recursion.

problems.title: Balanced Binary Tree
problems.description:
A binary tree is height-balanced if, for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Return `true` if the given tree is height-balanced.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Checking height separately at every node works but repeats a lot of work.
Compute heights bottom-up and report imbalance as soon as it is found, instead of recomputing heights top-down.
Process nodes in post-order. For each node compute height = 1 + max(hl, hr) and fail if |hl - hr| > 1.

problems.title: Subtree of Another Tree
problems.description:
Given two binary trees `root` and `sub_root`, return `true` if `root` contains a node whose entire subtree (that node and all its descendants) is identical in structure and values to `sub_root`.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Node 4 has an extra descendant, so its subtree is not identical.

constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each tree <= 2000
An empty `sub_root` is a subtree of every tree.
problems.complexity: O(n * m) time worst case, O(h) space
hints: Try every node of the big tree as a possible match point.
At each node, run a full 'same tree' comparison against sub_root. A match must cover the whole subtree, not just a prefix.
Traverse root; for every node whose value equals sub_root's root value, call same(node, sub_root). Return true on the first success.

problems.title: Path Sum
problems.description:
Return `true` if the tree has a root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to `target_sum`. A leaf is a node with no children, and the path must end at a leaf.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Root-to-leaf sums are 3 and 4 only.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Carry the remaining sum down the tree as you go.
At a node, subtract its value from the target; when you reach a leaf, check whether exactly zero is left.
Iterative DFS with (node, remaining) pairs. Careful: a node with only one child is not a leaf, so an empty side does not end a path.

problems.title: Path Sum II
problems.description:
Return every root-to-leaf path whose values sum to `target_sum`. Each path is a list of node values from root to leaf. Report the paths in the order a left-before-right depth-first traversal finds them.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: No root-to-leaf path sums to 5.

problems.complexity: O(n^2) time worst case (copying paths), O(h) extra space
hints: You need the actual paths, not just a yes/no, so keep track of the current path.
Use DFS with a shared path list: push on entry, pop on exit (backtracking). Record a copy at leaves with the right sum.
Visit left before right so the output order is deterministic. Only record at true leaves (no children).

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.description:
Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom. At each depth you see the rightmost node of that level.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Level 3 shows 5 and 4; the rightmost is 4.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the widest level
hints: The answer has exactly one value per depth level.
Process the tree level by level; the visible node on each level is the last one in left-to-right order.
BFS with a queue: for each level, record the value of the final node. DFS visiting right before left also works, taking the first node seen at each new depth.

problems.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
problems.description:
In a binary tree, a node `x` is called good if no node on the path from the root to `x` has a value greater than `x`'s value. The root is always good. Return the number of good nodes.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Good nodes: 3 (root), 4, 5 and the left-left 3.

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Whether a node is good depends only on the path above it.
Carry the maximum value seen so far along the path as you descend.
DFS with (node, maxSoFar). If node.val >= maxSoFar count it; pass max(maxSoFar, node.val) to the children.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder
problems.description:
You are given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree whose node values are all distinct. Rebuild the tree and return it as a level-order array, using `null` for missing children and trimming trailing `null`s.

Preorder visits root, then left subtree, then right subtree. Inorder visits left subtree, then root, then right subtree. Both lists contain the same values. For example, preorder `[3,9,20,15,7]` and inorder `[9,3,15,20,7]` give `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Root 3; inorder splits into left [9] and right [15,20,7].

constraints: Node values are distinct integers in [-3000, 3000]
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: The first element of preorder is always the root of the current subtree.
Find the root in inorder: everything to its left belongs to the left subtree, everything to its right to the right subtree. A hash map from value to inorder index makes this lookup O(1).

Recursively build with index ranges: the left subtree size tells you how far to advance in preorder. Consume preorder with a running pointer, building left before right. Use an explicit stack if depth could be large.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.description:
Given a binary tree with distinct node values and two values `p` and `q` that both exist in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` in its subtree. A node counts as a descendant of itself, so if `p` is an ancestor of `q` the answer is `p`.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: 5 and 1 hang under different children of the root 3.
5 is an ancestor of 4, and a node is its own ancestor.

constraints: `p` and `q` both exist in the tree (they may be equal)
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: If you knew each node's parent and depth, finding where two upward paths meet would be easy.
Alternatively, recurse: a node is the answer if p and q are found in different subtrees (or the node itself is one of them and the other lies below).
Record parent pointers with a traversal, collect all ancestors of p (including p), then walk up from q until you hit one of them.

problems.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
problems.description:
Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree in zigzag fashion: the first level is read left to right, the second right to left, the third left to right again, and so on. Return a list of levels.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.

examples.explanation: Level 2 is [9,20] left to right, so it is reported as [20,9].

problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space
hints: Start from a normal level-order (BFS) traversal.
Keep a flag that flips after each level.
Gather each level's values left to right, then reverse that list when the flag says right-to-left. Do not change the order in which children are enqueued.

problems.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
problems.description:
Every node of the tree holds a single digit from `0` to `9`. Each root-to-leaf path spells a number by concatenating the digits along it, for example the path `1 -> 2 -> 3` is the number `123`. Return the sum of the numbers over all root-to-leaf paths.

Trees are given as level-order arrays where `null` marks a missing child (children of a `null` are not listed), for example `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]`.
constraints: The depth of the tree is at most 15
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space
hints: Going one level deeper multiplies the number so far by 10 and adds the new digit.
Pass the running number down during DFS instead of building strings.
At a leaf (no children), add the running value to the total. The total fits comfortably in a 64-bit integer.

problems.title: Clone Graph
problems.description:
You are given a connected undirected graph as an adjacency list: `adj[i]` lists the neighbors of node `i + 1` (nodes are labeled `1..n`, in the order given). Build a deep copy of the graph - brand new node objects with the same connections - and return it in the same adjacency-list format.

In an interview you would be handed a `Node` class and a reference to one node; here, build the copy internally with your own node objects and serialize it at the end. The returned neighbor lists must keep the same neighbor order as the input. An empty graph is `[]`.
constraints: Node labels are 1..n and the graph is connected and simple (no self-loops or repeated edges)
Edges are undirected: if `a` is in `adj[b-1]` then `b` is in `adj[a-1]`
problems.complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V) space
hints: A plain traversal would visit nodes repeatedly in a cyclic graph; you must remember what you have already visited.
Keep a map from original node to its clone. When you first meet a node, create its clone and register it before exploring neighbors.

BFS/DFS from node 1: for each original node, for each neighbor, ensure the neighbor's clone exists (create and enqueue if not) and append it to the current clone's neighbor list. Finally serialize clones by label.

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.description:
A rectangular island is described by a grid `heights`, where `heights[r][c]` is the height of cell `(r, c)`. The Pacific ocean touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic ocean touches the bottom and right edges. Water on a cell can flow to any of its four neighbors whose height is less than or equal to the current cell's height, and water on an edge cell flows into the adjacent ocean.

Return all cells `[r, c]` from which water can reach both oceans, sorted by row and then by column.

examples.explanation: The only cell touches both oceans.

problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
hints: Asking 'which cells reach the ocean' for every cell separately is far too slow.
Reverse the flow: start from the ocean borders and walk uphill (to neighbors with height >= current). Every cell you reach can flow down to that ocean.
Run one BFS/DFS from all Pacific-border cells and one from all Atlantic-border cells; the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets, listed row-major.

solutions.python:
def pacific_atlantic(heights):
    m, n = len(heights), len(heights[0])

    def reach(starts):
        seen = set(starts)
        stack = list(starts)
        while stack:
            r, c = stack.pop()
            for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and (nr, nc) not in seen and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]:
                    seen.add((nr, nc))
                    stack.append((nr, nc))
        return seen

    pac = [(0, c) for c in range(n)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(1, m)]
    atl = [(m - 1, c) for c in range(n)] + [(r, n - 1) for r in range(m - 1)]
    both = reach(pac) & reach(atl)
    return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(both)]

problems.title: Surrounded Regions
problems.description:
You are given a board of `"X"` and `"O"` strings. A region is a group of `"O"` cells connected horizontally or vertically. A region is surrounded if none of its cells lies on the border of the board. Capture every surrounded region by turning all of its `"O"` cells into `"X"`. Regions that touch the border (and everything connected to them) stay unchanged.

Return the resulting board.

examples.explanation: The 'O' in the bottom row touches the border, so it stays.

problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
hints: Deciding whether a region is surrounded cell by cell is awkward - think about which cells are safe instead.
Any 'O' connected to a border 'O' is safe. Mark all safe cells first, starting from the border.
Flood fill from every border 'O' marking cells safe, then sweep the board: unsafe 'O' becomes 'X', safe cells stay 'O'.

problems.title: Walls and Gates
problems.description:
You are given a grid of rooms with three kinds of cells: `-1` is a wall, `0` is a gate, and `2147483647` (call it INF) is an empty room. Fill every empty room with the number of steps to its nearest gate, moving up, down, left or right and never through walls. Rooms that cannot reach any gate stay `2147483647`.

Return the updated grid.

examples.explanation: A lone gate stays 0.

problems.complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
hints: Running a search from every room to find a gate is wasteful.
Flip the viewpoint: start from all gates simultaneously and spread outward one step at a time.

Multi-source BFS: enqueue every gate with distance 0. When you pop a cell, any neighbor still equal to INF gets distance + 1 and is enqueued. The first time a room is reached is its shortest distance.

solutions.python:
from collections import deque


def walls_and_gates(rooms):
    INF = 2147483647
    grid = [row[:] for row in rooms]
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    q = deque((r, c) for r in range(m) for c in range(n) if grid[r][c] == 0)
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == INF:
                grid[nr][nc] = grid[r][c] + 1
                q.append((nr, nc))
    return grid

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.description: There are `num_courses` courses labeled `0..num_courses-1`. Each entry `[a, b]` of `prerequisites` means you must finish course `b` before taking course `a`. Return an order in which you can take all courses. Because many valid orders can exist, return the lexicographically smallest one (compare the lists element by element). If it is impossible to finish all courses because of a cycle, return an empty list.

examples.explanation: 0, then 1 and 2 are both available; the smaller (1) goes first.

constraints: Every pair is distinct and `a != b`
problems.complexity: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space
hints: This is a topological sort; a cycle means no order exists.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a course whose prerequisites are all done and reduce the in-degree of the courses it unlocks.
To get the lexicographically smallest order, always pick the smallest available course: keep the zero-in-degree courses in a min-heap. If fewer than num_courses courses are output, there is a cycle.

solutions.python:
import heapq


def find_order(num_courses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indeg = [0] * num_courses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    heap = [i for i in range(num_courses) if indeg[i] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    order = []
    while heap:
        u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(heap, v)
    return order if len(order) == num_courses else []

problems.title: Graph Valid Tree
problems.description: You have `n` nodes labeled `0..n-1` and a list of undirected `edges`. Return `true` if these edges make the graph a valid tree: connected and containing no cycles.

examples.explanation: Edges 1-2, 2-3, 1-3 form a cycle.

constraints: No self-loops; the same edge is not repeated in opposite orientation unless it is a deliberate duplicate
problems.complexity: O(n * alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
hints: A tree on n nodes has a very specific number of edges.
If edges != n - 1 the answer is false right away. Otherwise you only need to rule out a cycle (a connected check then follows automatically) or check connectivity.
With exactly n - 1 edges, use union-find: if any edge joins two nodes already in the same set, there is a cycle, so return false. Otherwise it is a tree.

problems.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problems.description: Given `n` nodes labeled `0..n-1` and a list of undirected `edges`, return the number of connected components in the graph. Isolated nodes count as components of their own.

examples.explanation: Components: {0,1,2} and {3,4}.

constraints: Edges may be listed more than once in either direction
problems.complexity: O((n + e) * alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
hints: Each time two separate groups get joined, the number of groups drops by one.
Start with n components. For every edge, merge the two endpoints' groups if they are different.
Union-find with path compression: components = n - (number of successful unions). A DFS/BFS with a visited array works too.

problems.title: Minimum Height Trees
problems.description: A tree is an undirected connected graph with no cycles. Given a tree of `n` nodes labeled `0..n-1` as a list of `edges`, you may pick any node as the root. The height of the rooted tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down. Return all root labels that give the minimum possible height, in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Rooting at node 1 gives height 1; any other root is worse.

constraints: The input is guaranteed to be a tree
problems.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
hints: There are never more than two answers, and they sit in the middle of the tree.
Think of peeling the tree like an onion: repeatedly remove all leaves.

Compute degrees, queue all leaves, and remove them layer by layer (decrementing neighbors' degrees; neighbors that become leaves join the next layer). Stop when 2 or fewer nodes remain; those are the answer. Handle n = 1 (answer `[0]`) and sort the result.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.description: There are `n` cities labeled `0..n-1`. Each entry `[from, to, price]` of `flights` is a one-way flight. Return the cheapest total price to travel from `src` to `dst` using at most `k` stops, where a stop is an intermediate city (so at most `k + 1` flights). If no such trip exists, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Best with one stop: 0 -> 1 -> 3 costs 700.
With one stop, 0 -> 1 -> 2 costs 200 which beats the direct 500.

constraints: `src != dst`, 0 <= k < n, prices are positive integers up to 10^4
problems.complexity: O(k * E) time, O(n) space
hints: The cheapest path overall may use too many flights, so plain Dijkstra on cost alone is not enough.
Limit the number of edges: after i rounds you only know the best prices that use at most i flights.
Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds. In each round, relax every flight using a copy of the previous round's distances (so one round adds at most one flight). Answer is dist[dst], or -1 if still infinite.

problems.title: Swim in Rising Water
problems.description:
You are given a square `grid` of side `n` that contains every integer from `0` to `n*n - 1` exactly once; `grid[r][c]` is the elevation of cell `(r, c)`. At time `t` the water level everywhere is `t`. You may move between two 4-directionally adjacent cells if both of their elevations are at most `t`. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell. Moving is instant, but you can only stand in cells already submerged (elevation <= t).

Return the smallest time `t` at which you can get from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.

examples.explanation: At t=3 the whole grid is passable; at t=2 the bottom-right cell (3) is still dry.

problems.complexity: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
hints: The time you need equals the highest elevation you must pass through on your best route.
That is a minimax path problem: minimize the maximum cell value along a path.

Dijkstra with a min-heap keyed on the largest elevation seen so far on the path: pop the cell with the smallest bottleneck, update neighbors with max(current bottleneck, neighbor elevation). Binary search on t plus BFS also works.

problems.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.description:
You have a list of airline `tickets`, each `[from, to]` using 3-letter uppercase airport codes. Rebuild the itinerary that starts at `"JFK"` and uses every ticket exactly once. A valid itinerary is guaranteed to exist.

If several valid itineraries exist, return the one that is smallest in lexicographic order when compared airport by airport. For example `["JFK","LGA",...]` comes before `["JFK","LGB",...]`.

examples.explanation: The only valid chain is JFK -> MUC -> LHR -> SFO -> SJC.
Going to ATL first works: JFK -> ATL -> JFK -> SFO -> ATL -> SFO.

constraints: Airport codes are 3 uppercase letters; the same ticket can appear more than once
A valid itinerary using every ticket exactly once is guaranteed
problems.complexity: O(E log E) time, O(E) space
hints: Every ticket must be used exactly once - this is an Eulerian path problem.
A greedy 'always take the smallest next airport' can get stuck at a dead end before all tickets are used.

Hierholzer's algorithm: keep each airport's destinations sorted; DFS taking the smallest unused destination; append an airport to the route only when it has no more outgoing tickets, then reverse the route at the end.

problems.title: Accounts Merge
problems.description:
Each entry of `accounts` is a list whose first element is a person's name and whose remaining elements are email addresses belonging to that account. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email address. Names alone never prove two accounts are the same person - different people may share a name - but accounts that share an email always have the same name.

Merge the accounts. Return one list per person: the name followed by that person's distinct emails in ascending (lexicographic) order. Return the list of merged accounts sorted lexicographically, comparing the lists element by element (name first, then emails).

examples.explanation: The first two Johns share johnsmith@mail.com; the third John is a different person.

constraints: Each account has a name followed by 1 to 10 emails
Names are letters only; emails are lowercase-style strings (letters, digits, `@`, `.`, `_`)
Every account has at least one email
problems.complexity: O(N log N) time where N is the total number of emails, O(N) space
hints: Emails are the real identity; accounts are just bags of emails linking them together.
Treat each email as a node and connect all emails inside the same account. Each connected group is one person.
Union-find over emails (map email -> id, remember email -> name). After all unions, group emails by root, sort each group, prepend the name, and sort the final list.

problems.title: Evaluate Division
problems.description:
You are given equations of the form `A / B = value` as `equations[i] = [A, B]` and `values[i]`. All variables are strings and the equations are consistent (no contradictions). Answer each query `[C, D]` by computing `C / D` using the known equations, or `-1.0` if the answer cannot be determined (including when a variable never appears in the equations). A variable divided by itself is `1.0` if it appears in the equations.

Return the answers as floating-point numbers rounded to 5 decimal places.

examples.explanation: a/c = 2 * 3 = 6; b/a = 0.5; e is unknown; a/a = 1; x never appears.

problems.complexity: O(Q * (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space
hints: Think of each variable as a node and each equation as a weighted edge, in both directions (A/B = x means B/A = 1/x).
Dividing C by D means multiplying the edge weights along any path from C to D.
Build the adjacency map with weights x and 1/x. For each query, BFS/DFS from C to D multiplying weights; return -1.0 if either node is unknown or D is unreachable. Round each answer to 5 decimals.

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
problems.description:
You have a collection of stones with positive integer weights. Each turn, take the two heaviest stones and smash them together. If their weights are equal, both are destroyed. Otherwise the lighter one is destroyed and the heavier one is reduced to the difference of the two weights. Continue until at most one stone remains.

Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or `0` if no stones remain.

examples.explanation: Smash 8 and 7 to get 1, then 4 and 2 to get 2, and so on until one stone of weight 1 remains.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: Each step needs the two largest elements, and the collection keeps changing.
A max-heap gives you the largest element in O(log n) and lets you push the difference back.
Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated weights. Loop while the heap has at least two stones: pop two, push their difference if it is nonzero.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.description: Given a list of lowercase `words` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent words. Sort the result by frequency from highest to lowest; words with the same frequency are ordered alphabetically (lexicographically smaller first).

examples.explanation: `i` and `love` both appear twice; `i` is alphabetically first.

constraints: words[i] are non-empty lowercase strings (letters and digits)
problems.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(n) space
hints: Count the occurrences of every word first.
Ranking is by (higher count first, then smaller word first). You only need the best k, not a full sort.

Keep a heap of size k whose top is the worst candidate (lower count, or equal count and larger word). Push each (word, count); when the heap exceeds k, pop the worst. Finally sort the survivors best-first.

solutions.python:
import heapq
from collections import Counter


def top_k_frequent_words(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return [w for w, _ in best]

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.description:
Design a structure that tracks the `k`-th largest element of a growing collection (the k-th largest in sorted order, counting duplicates). It starts with the numbers in `nums`, then receives the values in `adds` one at a time. Simulate it: after each add, record the current k-th largest, and return all recorded values as a list.

It is guaranteed that `nums.length + 1 >= k`, so the k-th largest exists after every add.

examples.explanation: Sorted after first add: [2,3,4,5,8]; 3rd largest is 4.

problems.complexity: O((n + m) log k) time, O(k) space
hints: You never need elements outside the current top k.
Keep a min-heap containing only the k largest values seen so far; its smallest element is the k-th largest overall.
On each add: push the value; if the heap has more than k items, pop the minimum. Then the heap's top is the answer for that step.

problems.title: Find the Town Judge
problems.description:
In a town of `n` people labeled `1..n` there may be a secret judge. If the judge exists, then (1) the judge trusts nobody, and (2) everybody else trusts the judge. Exactly one person can satisfy both conditions.

You are given `trust`, where each `[a, b]` means person `a` trusts person `b`. Return the label of the judge, or `-1` if there is none.

examples.explanation: Person 3 is trusted by both others and trusts nobody.

constraints: All pairs are distinct and `a != b`
problems.complexity: O(n + t) time, O(n) space
hints: Each person has some number of people trusting them and some number of people they trust.
The judge is trusted by exactly n - 1 people and trusts exactly 0.
Keep one counter per person: +1 when trusted, -1 when trusting. The judge is the person whose score is n - 1. Return -1 if nobody has it.
